text: Dijkstra with a heap; layered graphs.
d = 3 thick: shortest-path tree

Dijkstra (non-negative weights): keep tentative distances d[]. Repeatedly take the unfinished node u with the smallest d, mark it finished, and relax its edges: d[v] = min(d[v], d[u] + w). A priority queue finds u in O(log n), so the whole run is O(m log m).

Why it is right: when u has the smallest d among unfinished nodes, any other route to u must leave the finished set through a node already at least d[u] away, and adding non-negative edges cannot make it shorter. A negative edge breaks this argument.

Instead of decreasing a key, push a new pair and skip outdated ones with done[u] . The queue holds at most m entries (P4779).
Unreachable nodes keep LLONG_MAX: never add to it (overflow). Print them as the problem asks. Dense graphs with n ≤ 5000 can use the O(n²) version without a heap.
Counting shortest paths (P1144): when dist[u] + w == dist[v], add cnt[u] to cnt[v]; when it is smaller, reset cnt[v] = cnt[u]. Done nodes come out in distance order, so counts are final.

Layered graph (分层图): when the route also has a small counter (free flights used, keys held, fuel), make the state (node, counter). Each layer is a copy of the graph; a free flight is an edge of weight 0 into the next layer (P4568).

States: n·(k + 1); edges: about 2m·(k + 1). Any shortest path idea works on the state graph unchanged. "Minimise the largest toll on the way, with a budget" (P1462) binary searches the toll and runs Dijkstra on the allowed edges.
Bellman-Ford / SPFA, negative cycles, inequality systems.

With negative edges use Bellman-Ford: relax every edge, n − 1 rounds. A shortest path has at most n − 1 edges, so that is enough, unless a negative cycle is reachable: then distances keep falling forever. SPFA relaxes only from nodes whose distance just changed, using a queue.

Negative cycle test with SPFA: keep cnt[v] = number of edges on the current shortest path to v. If cnt[v] reaches n, the path repeats a node, so a negative cycle exists. SPFA is O(nm) in the worst case: use it only where negative edges force you to.
YES NO

Only cycles reachable from the start are found, because only those nodes ever get a finite distance (P3385 asks exactly this). To find any negative cycle at all, start from a super source joined to every node by a 0 edge.
Count edges (cnt[v] = cnt[u] + 1), not how many times v was queued: a node can be pushed many times without any cycle, and the queue count needs n + 1, not n.
NO

A system of inequalities xa − xb ≤ c looks like the shortest-path rule d[a] ≤ d[b] + w. So add an edge b → a of weight c, run shortest paths from a super source, and d[] is a solution. A negative cycle means no solution (P5960).
Rewrite other forms first: xa − xb ≥ c becomes xb − xa ≤ −c; xa = xb is two ≤ 0 edges; xa < xb on integers is xa − xb ≤ −1 (P1993, P3275 糖果 uses longest paths for the minimum total).
Two distances per node.

The second shortest path (次短路): keep two values per node, d1[v] the shortest and d2[v] the strictly second shortest. A candidate length L at v either beats d1 (old d1 slides down to d2) or lies strictly between d1 and d2. Both changes are pushed into the queue (P2865).
A node may now be taken from the queue twice (once per value), so do not use a done[] array: skip an entry only when its length exceeds d2[v]. Paths may reuse edges, which the problem allows here.

The swap does both jobs at once: after a new best is stored, L holds the old best, which then gets the "strictly between" test. Shortest 1 → 2 → 4 is 300; second is 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 = 450.

Another way: Dijkstra from 1 and from n, then for every edge (u, v, w) the best path through it is d1[u] + w + dn[v]; the smallest value above the shortest is the answer. The same "from both ends" trick solves 最优贸易(P1073) on a forward and a reversed graph.

title: 多源最短路径与传递闭包

text: Floyd and reachability.

Floyd computes all-pairs shortest paths in O(n³): for k = 1 … n, allow node k as a middle stop: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]). After round k, d[i][j] is the shortest path whose middle nodes are all in {1, …, k}.
The k loop must be outermost. Floyd handles negative edges (not negative cycles: some d[i][i] < 0 reveals one). Use it when n ≤ 400 or so, or when every pair is needed.

Transitive closure (传递闭包) is Floyd with "or / and" instead of "min / +": can i reach j? (B3611). A cow's rank is fixed exactly when every other cow is comparable to it (P2419). With bitset<N> rows, "if beat[i][k] then row i |= row k" is n³ / 64.

Floyd's order is a tool: in 灾后重建(P1119) villages are rebuilt in time order, so process k in that order and answer each query once its time is reached. Counting shortest paths through each node (P2047 社交网络) keeps a count matrix next to d.
